story962:
In the beginning, there was nothing but water covering everything. A man carrying a Flat Pipe walked on the water for six days, weeping and fasting, searching for a safe place to rest his pipe. On the sixth day, a water bird took pity on him and called to the other animals.

The animals gathered in council. The diver dove deep, seeking mud from the bottom of the endless ocean. It failed — the water was too deep. The beaver tried next, its powerful tail driving it downward through the black water. It surfaced empty-pawed. The loon, the muskrat, all tried. All failed.

At last the toad, smallest and humblest of all the animals, offered to try. It dove into the water and was gone so long that the others assumed it had drowned. But at last it surfaced, its body bloated, its eyes bulging — and in its paw, a tiny clump of mud.

The man took the mud and placed it on the back of a giant turtle that had risen from the depths. He spread the mud across the turtle's shell, singing as he worked. The mud grew and spread, becoming an island, then a continent. The man set down his Flat Pipe and wept with gratitude.

The Flat Pipe became the center of Arapaho spiritual life. It was kept wrapped in skin and fur, its power immense but dormant — a connection to the moment when the world was created from nothing but water and a single act of courage.
story963:
Nihancan is the Arapaho trickster figure, a spider-like being similar to Iktomi of the Lakota and Wihio of the Cheyenne. He is both clever and foolish, often causing trouble through his greed and selfishness, but sometimes inadvertently benefiting the people.

Nihancan's adventures are both humorous and instructive. In one tale, he tricked the birds into a dance and wrung their necks — a story that mirrors Wenebojo's treachery among the Ojibwe. In another, he tried to steal fire from the fire spirits but ended up burning his own tail, which is why spiders have such thin legs.

Nihancan was not evil. He was simply driven by appetites that overrode his judgment. He wanted everything for himself and could not understand why the world did not rearrange itself to suit his desires. His failures taught the people what not to do — how greed leads to ruin, how selfishness alienates allies, how carelessness brings disaster.

But Nihancan also had a creative side. Through his mistakes, he inadvertently shaped the world. The rivers flowed in their current courses because Nihancan dug them and then forgot to fill them back in. The trees grew with their branches reaching upward because Nihancan tried to climb them and bent them in the process.

The people told Nihancan stories not to mock him but to learn from him. Every person carried a bit of Nihancan within — the part that wanted too much, that acted without thinking, that assumed the best without preparing for the worst. By laughing at Nihancan, they learned to laugh at themselves.
story964:
Found-in-the-Grass is a rags-to-riches hero of Arapaho folklore. In some versions, he is an orphan abandoned as an infant and found by villagers in the tall grass. In others, he is the magical twin Spirit-in-the-Water, who received supernatural powers after a vision quest.

As a child, Found-in-the-Grass was mocked by the other children. He was small, dirty, and poorly dressed. His clothes were rags, his hair was tangled, and he had no parents to defend him. The children threw stones at him and chased him from their games.

But Found-in-the-Grass had a secret. He had been visited in a dream by a powerful spirit who gave him a magical robe. When he wore the robe, he became invisible. When he spoke, his words carried the weight of prophecy. When he sang, the animals gathered to listen.

As he grew older, the villagers began to recognize his power. He led successful hunts, predicted storms, healed the sick. The same children who had mocked him now sought his counsel. He married the chief's daughter, built a great lodge, and became one of the most respected leaders of his people.

The story teaches that dignity and worth are not determined by circumstances of birth or appearance. The child who was found in the grass became the man who led the people — not because of his origins but because of his character.
story965:
A childless Arapaho woman found a splinter embedded in her foot. To her amazement, the splinter grew and transformed into a baby girl. The girl grew rapidly and possessed supernatural abilities. She could talk to animals, command the wind, and make things appear and disappear with a word.

The woman loved the girl as her own daughter and raised her with care. But as the girl grew older, her powers became more difficult to control. She accidentally killed a buffalo with a glance, set a forest ablaze with a laugh, and caused a river to change course with a frown.

The medicine men of the village were frightened. They said the girl was too powerful to live among humans. They urged her mother to send her away.

But the mother refused. "She is my daughter," she said. "I will not abandon her."

The girl heard this and was moved. She gathered her power and used it to benefit the people — bringing rain in times of drought, guiding hunters to game, healing the wounded. She became a protector of the village, her power tempered by the love her mother had shown her.

The story teaches that love can tame even the most dangerous power, and that rejection creates monsters while acceptance creates heroes.
story966:
An Arapaho girl was picking berries when she saw a porcupine in a tree. She climbed after it, but the tree grew taller and taller, carrying her into the sky world. In the sky, she found a beautiful land of eternal summer — green grass, flowing water, animals that spoke with human voices.

The sky people welcomed her. They fed her, clothed her, and gave her a place to live. But they warned her: "Do not look down at the earth. If you look down, you will fall."

The girl lived happily in the sky for a time. She married a sky man, had children, and learned the songs of the wind. But she missed her people on the earth below. She missed the taste of wild berries, the sound of the river, the warmth of the sun on her face.

One day, she looked down.

The ground rushed up to meet her. She fell through the sky, past the clouds, past the birds, past the wind. She fell so fast that the air burned her skin and tore her clothes. She screamed, but no one could hear her.

At the last moment, a great eagle caught her in its talons and set her gently on the ground. She landed in the village of her people, who had mourned her for years. She told them of the sky world and returned to live among them.

The story teaches that curiosity has consequences, but also that the spirits are merciful. The girl's fall was not punished — it was redirected. She returned to the earth a wiser woman, carrying the songs of the sky in her heart.
story967:
The Arapaho Sun Dance, known as the Offerings Lodge, is a central spiritual ceremony. Unlike other Plains tribes that practiced self-torture, the Arapaho version involved donating personal items, spending time in isolation, and making offerings to the Creator.

The ceremony took place in a specially constructed lodge — a circular structure of poles and buffalo hides, open at the top to the sky. The center pole, the tallest of all, represented the connection between the earth and the heavens. It was the axis mundi, the point where the human world met the divine.

For four days, the participants danced and prayed in the lodge. They gave away their possessions — blankets, weapons, tools, food. They offered their labor and their sweat to the Creator. They fasted and spoke with the spirits.

The Sun Dance was not a spectacle but a deeply personal experience. Each dancer had their own reasons for participating — to heal a sick child, to ensure a successful hunt, to fulfill a vow made in desperation. The ceremony was their direct communication with the Creator, a moment when the barriers between the human and divine dissolved.

The Arapaho Sun Dance was nearly destroyed by the U.S. government, which banned it along with other Native religious practices in the late 19th century. But the ceremony survived underground, passed from elder to elder in secret. When the ban was finally lifted, the Sun Dance was revived, and today it remains the most important ceremony in the Arapaho calendar.
story968:
During a terrible famine, all the buffalo had disappeared from the plains. The Arapaho people were starving. A powerful medicine man went into the mountains to seek a vision. After four days of fasting and prayer, a spirit appeared to him — a great buffalo bull whose body filled the sky.

The spirit spoke: "The buffalo have not gone. They are hiding beneath the earth, in a great cave. You must lead your people to the cave and perform the sacred songs. Then the buffalo will return."

The medicine man returned to his people and led them to the place the spirit had shown him. At the base of a great cliff, they found the entrance to a cave — dark, cold, and deep. The medicine man entered alone, singing the sacred songs as he descended.

Inside the cave, he found the buffalo — thousands of them, their eyes gleaming in the darkness, their breath steaming in the cold. They stood in silence, waiting. The medicine man sang louder, and the buffalo began to move. They walked toward the entrance, one by one, until the cave was empty and the plains were full.

The buffalo returned to the grasslands, and the Arapaho people were saved. The medicine man was honored for the rest of his life, and the songs he sang in the cave were preserved as some of the most sacred in the Arapaho tradition.
story969:
A lame Arapaho warrior, unable to fight alongside his people, was left behind when the village moved. As he sat alone, a skeleton approached him. The skeleton offered to carry the warrior to battle if the warrior would promise to share half of everything he gained.

The warrior agreed. The skeleton carried him across the plains at incredible speed — faster than any horse, faster than the wind. They arrived at the enemy camp just as the battle began. The warrior fought bravely, his legs healed by the skeleton's magic, and won great glory.

But when he returned, the skeleton came to collect its share. The warrior had promised half of everything. The skeleton took half his horses, half his weapons, half his food. Then it said, "Now I will take half of you."

The warrior was terrified. But the skeleton only took his memory of the battle — the warrior could no longer remember his greatest victory. He knew he had won but could not recall the details, the excitement, the pride.

The story teaches the danger of making deals with supernatural beings. The skeleton kept its word — it took exactly half of everything. But the warrior learned too late that some things are worth more than horses or weapons. A memory of one's greatest moment is priceless, and giving it away is the greatest loss of all.
story970:
Nihancan the trickster was wandering when he encountered a small dwarf armed with a bow and arrow. Nihancan laughed at the dwarf, mocking his small size and tiny weapon. "What could you possibly do with that toy?" he said.

The dwarf challenged Nihancan to a contest. Nihancan agreed, certain he would win. The dwarf shot an arrow into the sky, and it flew higher than any arrow Nihancan had ever seen — so high it disappeared into the sun.

Nihancan was impressed despite himself. "Let me try," he said. He took the dwarf's bow and shot an arrow with all his strength. The arrow flew high but not as high as the dwarf's. It fell back to earth and struck Nihancan on the head.

Nihancan was furious. He grabbed the dwarf and squeezed him, trying to crush him. But the dwarf transformed into a snake and slithered away. Nihancan grabbed the snake, but it transformed into a bird and flew away. Nihancan grabbed the bird, but it transformed into a fish and swam away.

Nihancan sat alone on the plain, defeated and humbled. He had mocked the dwarf for being small, but the dwarf had outwitted him at every turn. The story teaches that size and appearance are no measure of power, and that the greatest mistake is to underestimate those who are different from oneself.
